newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schaeuble defends Bonn's reform efforts.
newsitem.headline: Schaeuble defends Bonn's reform efforts.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's top deputy said on Monday the centre-right government had pushed through many reforms in the last 16 months and said the widespread public impression of political logjam was wrong.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, leader of the Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) parliamentary group, said he welcomed comments from President Roman Herzog, who accused legislators of failing to tackle overdue reforms of tax, pension and labour laws.
"The President's speech was excellent and welcome," Schaeuble told a news conference. "But he wasn't only addressing politicians, he was also talking about lobbyists."

Schaeuble said that the centre-right government had made important breakthroughs with its efforts to stimulate job creation in the economy since embarking on a reform drive at the beginning of last year.
"There is an impression we have run into a logjam," he said.
"That impression is wrong. We have accomplished a tremendous amount since January 1996 and we will take all necessary steps."

He said new laws liberalising shop open hours, limiting sick pay benefits and making it easier to lay off workers in smaller companies were some of the areas where the government had taken steps to boost the economy.
"There is no reform logjam," Schaeuble said before blaming journalists for saying there was. "You are also to blame for the wrong impression if you report that."
Schaeuble blamed the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) for the collapse last week of talks on sweeping tax reform plans.
He said the government would press ahead with reforms in areas where the SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, are powerless to block the legislation.
"Even if the SPD sticks with its blockade policies, there will be no political logjam," he said. But he also blasted the SPD for changing its position on various corporate taxes.
"The SPD changes its opinion on taxes as much as some other people change their underwear," Schaeuble said.
Herzog, whose largely ceremonial office is above partisan wrangling, scolded the whole political class in a hard-hitting speech in Berlin on Saturday.
